query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Doping the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst with a low level of cerium followed by a controlled mild oxidation treatment will form surface CeOx species that improve low-temperature oxidation activity, resist poisoning by H2O and NO, and enhance catalyst durability compared to the unmodified catalyst.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst with minimal platinum-group-metal content that experiences reduced performance during low-temperature transient operation and after prolonged aging.
generation.intervention: Doping with a low concentration of cerium and applying a mild oxidation treatment to generate surface CeOx.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions with temperatures below 150 °C, presence of H2O and NO, and accelerated aging protocols that mimic vehicle lifetime mileage degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale CeOx patches forming on the catalyst surface and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The CeOx species enhance oxygen storage and facilitate oxygen mobility, aiding CO and hydrocarbon oxidation at low temperatures while hindering the adsorption or deactivation from poisoning species, and also mitigating sintering during aging.
generation.predicted_outcome: The cerium-doped catalyst is expected to exhibit lower light-off temperatures, improved conversion efficiencies in the presence of poisons, and higher performance retention after aging relative to the unmodified catalyst.
generation.baseline: The unmodified multi‐principal‐element catalyst shows diminished low-temperature oxidation activity and durability under simulated transient exhaust and aging conditions.
generation.boundary: These improvements are anticipated under typical automotive exhaust environments with low platinum-group-metal use; however, effects at extreme or heavily fluctuating conditions may vary.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal cerium concentration and the exact magnitude of the performance enhancement across all realistic exhaust conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of catalysts: one with the base near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element composition and one doped with a low level of cerium followed by mild oxidation. Expose both groups to simulated automotive exhaust conditions (temperatures below 150 °C with H2O and NO) combined with accelerated aging cycles representative of vehicle lifetime mileage degradation.
measurements: CO oxidation rate and light-off temperature measurements
Hydrocarbon oxidation efficiency in the presence of H2O and NO
Performance retention after accelerated aging cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cerium-doped catalyst does not show statistically significant lower light-off temperatures, reduced poisoning-induced deactivation, and improved retention of oxidation activity compared to the baseline under the defined test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Incorporating a low concentration of cerium into the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst—and then using a mild oxidation treatment to generate surface CeOx—will enhance low-temperature oxidation activity, improve resistance to poisoning by species such as H2O and NO, and extend catalyst lifetime without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
drafts.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst with low platinum-group-metal use that exhibits declining performance during low-temperature transient operation and aging.
drafts.intervention: Doping with a small amount of cerium followed by controlled mild oxidation to form CeOx at the catalyst surface.
drafts.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions featuring low temperatures (below 150 °C), the presence of H2O and NO, and accelerated aging cycles that mimic lifetime mileage degradation.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale CeOx patches or nanoclusters at active sites and grain boundaries which improve oxygen storage and transport.
drafts.mechanism: CeOx can facilitate oxygen mobility and redox cycling, promoting CO and hydrocarbon oxidation at lower temperatures while also mitigating the adsorption or deactivation effects of poisoning species like H2O and NO. The CeOx enrichment at the surface is expected to stabilize the active phase against sintering and degradation during prolonged use.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the Ce-doped catalyst is expected to exhibit lower light-off temperatures (i.e., improved low-temperature activity), maintain higher conversion efficiencies in the presence of poisons, and retain its performance after extensive aging.
drafts.baseline: The original multi-principal-element alloy catalyst shows a reduction in oxidation performance and durability during transient, low-temperature conditions and accelerated aging.
drafts.boundary: This improvement is anticipated under typical automotive exhaust conditions with low platinum-group-metal content; however, the optimal Ce concentration and exact benefits might vary and may not extend to extreme exhaust environments outside the tested parameter space.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one comprising the baseline near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element alloy and one with a low-level cerium doping followed by mild oxidation processing. Expose both sets to simulated automotive exhaust conditions featuring temperatures below 150 °C, with added H2O and NO, along with a series of accelerated aging cycles (designed to mimic vehicle lifetime mileage). Compare the catalysts’ oxidation rates for CO and hydrocarbons before and after aging.
measurements: CO conversion rate at temperatures below 150 °C
Degree of deactivation by H2O and NO (measured as a percentage drop in activity)
Performance retention after accelerated aging tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cerium-doped catalyst does not exhibit statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower light-off temperature, reduced poisoning-induced deactivation, and higher retention of activity post-aging) compared to the baseline catalyst under the defined conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
